Tell HN: Bob Cringely has died
886 points by paveworld 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 191 comments

I heard from a friend of the family that Bob passed away in his sleep early Saturday. Very sad news. Bob, who's real name was Mark Stevens, was an early employee of Apple and was best known for his PBS documentaries, especially "Triumph of the Nerds". He will be missed.

This is an amazing show.

If you're familiar with it, maybe you could answer one question: Cringely sourced a lot of the materials and know-how for the plane from American companies and workers. Would that be possible today?

Yes, there are quite a few American companies making light sport and experimental aircraft, they are just very small and cater to a mostly wealthy hobby market. Lots of composites still being made here as well.

Everyone he talks to keeps saying that it can't be done and he goes for it anyway only to realize that they were all right. Even though the actual project is an abject failure it's still very entertaining.

I found a better rip of the documentary midway through this archive.org upload of off-air PBS recordings from North Carolina: https://archive.org/details/unc-tv-1997-vhs-720p-60 . It took like an hour to download and the tape hiss was pretty bad, so I ran it through Final Cut Pro's audio denoising filter and reuploaded it to Youtube here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rqxU4nnLkeA

https://www.jeremyreimer.com/rockets-item.lsp?f=true&p=272 makes it sound like the "crazy shit over the last few years" wasn't rue.

The post makes a strong case that the cataracts story and the losing his house story were false, among others.

If you're wondering why someone would make things like this up, it appears that they were cover stories for his Mineserver Kickstarter never shipping despite him saying "[i]n terms of development, this project was almost finished before the Kickstarter campaign began", "[a]ll these Mineservers will ship this week. Software is complete and SD cards are being duplicated. T-shirts are being printed every night", etc.

If it sounds unbelievable that someone would make these things up to have something to blame for a failed kickstarter, I recommend reading the post. The evidence against the house burning down is hard to argue with (later Google Maps/Street View imaging shows no apparent damage, in a later post he accidentally revealed that he used the exact laptop that he said he replaced because it was lost in the fire) and there's even stronger evidence that a number of his other claims are fabricated.

That kind of lying is what I sometimes expect from children under 10, it's shocking to me that an adult with some manner of family and career would behave in such a way, in so public a manner.

Thanks for that link. Completely changed my feelings about the guy, unfortunately for the worse, but in the end it's better to know.

I remember watching "Triumph of the Nerds" as a appx. 10 year old (it aired some years later in Norway). Two quotes stuck with me from that. The first is Ballmer mocking IBMers for bragging about how many KLOCs they had written every day. He's point being that the code is not the product. The other was Ellison complaining about the software distribution models at the time. "Don't put software on plastic discs, plastic discs in cardboard box, cardboard box in a warehouse and later in a store. Instead put the software on the net." I remember calculating how long it would be to download the full Windows 95 disc on my 28.8 modem, and thinking that it would be long time until that was feasible.

NerdTV: In an era of nascent web video, he produced long-form video interviews with tech types, and clipped what might now be called "Shorts/Tiktoks" from the conversations, pulling out the of "the juicy bit" and "the nerdy bit". https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NerdTV (h/t to u/Keyframe)

And obliquely, Cringely's columns or videos were the first place I recall hearing about foveated approaches to video compression for streaming. I thought it sounded like a terrible idea, but I guess Valve delivered, 20 years on, using the technique to good effect with the Steam Frame. Chalk one up for Cringely; RIP.

I really liked the guy, and his speculations about IBM.

But it's wild to get involved in a Kickstarter involving the star of Plane Crazy. When I watched Kickstarters fail and the people who started them grow increasingly unstable, I would always think about Plane Crazy.

Too bad that it didn't get a lot of distribution; there's a link on this HN thread pointing to a copy on youtube that was taped off PBS in Chicago, and I literally saw it on WTTW in Chicago. I don't know where it could really be marketed - it might be great to reedit it into a feature.

But its theme is that Cringely would bite off more than he can chew during what one might not recognize as a mania. You would see this pattern in almost everything he did, unless he was lucky enough to get it right on the first try.

1) he would make a lot of promises based on a dream of accomplishing something that no one had ever done before,

2) experts he would consult would tell him that they didn't think it was possible, but that they'd be happy to be surprised,

3) as the problems would pile up and he would gradually come to the realization that he was going to fail, he would first look at those problems as interesting challenges,

4) improvise inadequate solutions to show he could meet those challenges,

5) ignore the experts who criticize those inadequate solutions, and that tell him that these were the problems that made them think this was impossible in the first place,

6) mock and attack the experts who criticized his inadequate solutions (likely as stuck in the past or jealous of a non-expert invading their turf),

7) then start to conceal new and compounding problems,

8) then fully and knowingly lie about the problems (likely justified to himself as simply buying time for one fix he's obsessing upon to work),

9) then start to blame people who don't believe those lies for inadequately supporting him (he just needs a little bit more time),

10) then attack those people - his investors, friends and family (I just need another day or two!),

11) then attack himself for being low enough to attack the people who believe in him and love him,

12) then consider suicide.

Have there been any "Plane Crazy"-style documentaries about any of the spectacular Kickstarter failures?

The weird thing is that a lot of people that are ultimately successful share a lot of these traits. But I think the big differentiator is in how you deal with any of them, you can have the trait of not immediately rolling over when an expert says something can't be done. That's fine. But if ultimately you can't do it either you simply admit the experts were right after all and you move on. The further down the list you go the bigger the success if you eventually do manage to deliver, but the bigger the loss if you don't.

Where Cringely went from interesting to a risk to himself and others is where he refused to stay connected to reality.

I can relate: I start a lot of projects where I'm usually in over my head. But I always learn, sometimes learn a lot and some of those projects eventually do work out. But I don't have my ego invested in any project and I think that is one of the bigger differences, some stuff works and is obvious, some stuff could work and is not obvious, some stuff can't work but it is not obvious (to me at least) and some stuff simply can't work and it is obvious. The third category is where you lose the money, the second is where you make it, the dividing line between the two will give you Theranos, UBeam and Moller on one side of the line and CISCO on the other.

“well for a short time I was an employee of Apple Computer, employee number 12 and one day I helped move materials out of this garage. At the time Steve Jobs said that the company was short of loot so he offered to pay me in company shares, but I held out for the money - my mother still reminds me of that incident.”

Daniel Kottke was Employee #12 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Kottke

Cringely says here that he worked part-time at Apple for a few months as a graduate student: https://www.pbs.org/nerds/qa4.html . Mark Stephens was at Stanford at the time (he earned his master's in communication in 1979) so this lines up. I think it's entirely possible that Cringely/Stephens was in fact the 12th person hired by Apple, but didn’t get a formal employee number because he wasn't a full-time employee.

But Cringely stated on Triumph of the Nerds that he was literally "Employee #12". Other than this statement of his, there are no other sources to confirm that this was true. There's a very comprehensive list of early Apple employees with evidence to back them up here: https://apple.fandom.com/wiki/List_of_early_Apple_Computer_e...

Mark Stephens does not appear anywhere in this list, nor have any other early employees confirmed that he worked there.

Yes, this might have just been a small slip-up on Cringely's part, but the trouble is that he continued to make claims about being employed by Apple that were clearly fabricated. For example, Cringely claimed to have invented the Lisa's trash can icon in this clip: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=06M64l7pPIk&t=373s but if you read about the same story from other Apple employees, they don't mention him at all: https://folklore.org/Rosings_Rascals.html

These "tall tales" start to add up, and it becomes very hard to give him the benefit of the doubt.

Cringely was a great writer, a great documentarian, and really wonderful at finding the human stories behind the giants of the personal computer industry. Unfortunately, he also often made up stories about himself that were later found to be untrue. He didn't need to do this, because his work stood on its own. It was just a flaw in his personality.

In any case, this is sad news. Rest in peace, Mark Stephens.

That's fair, there's some other stuff that he seems to have verifiably lied about. There's the Lisa stuff you mention, and he lied about being a professor at Stanford when in reality he was either a TA or one level above a TA (sort of like Lex Fridman and MIT). I'm not sure that he'd lie altogether about being an early Apple employee when he was presenting a show that interviewed both Jobs and Wozniak (who would likely see the show and know that he was lying), but who knows.

You might already know this because you seem to know a lot about him, but when I was researching the Lisa claim you brought up I found a CHM oral history with Dan'l Lewin (https://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/20...), where page 20 mentions that Cringely was married to Ellen Nold while she was working on the Lisa project. Maybe that's how he got some of his anecdotes about Apple in the early 80s. EDIT: Cringely's next Apple anecdote in the talk you linked was about AppleLink, and this photo has Nold listed as manager of support programs for AppleLink: https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/ellen-nold-the...

I agree that his tendency to exaggerate his own past is unfortunate but doesn't outweigh all the great journalism he's done.

RIP. Damn and Dvorak died earlier this year? What a sad year for legendary computer columnists.

It's a pity that new media has never really thrown up a replacement for those sort of columnists, isn't it? Negroponte in Wired, Douglas Adams in MacUser, and (slightly more obscure!) Dave Langford's work in various Amstrad PCW magazines in the UK.

Slashdot did experiment a little with Jon Katz, most notably his 'Voices from the Hellmouth' series, but he was never really aiming to sound the same note of wry detachment as those magazine greats.

It's a pity - I'd rather read a monthly column of that sort than any amount of pointless bickering on Twitter.

To quote Fran Lebowtiz "A great audience is more important for the creation of great art than great artists are"... We've lost a great, ironic, self aware informed commentariat because a literate, emotionally stable audience for long form content has shrunk. Which means the work isn't there (or at least isn't distributed beyond a few substacks), to perpetuate and expand that audience.

I see the same effect all the time in fiction. Innovative challenging books don't get published (or even picked up by agents), because the publishing industry is run by the kind of people who are frightened and offended by such books. Which means the audience for those books become only those lucky enough to be exposed to older, denser, more innovative fiction - which invariably shrinks.

The latter were often written in a sort of gossipy style intended to make the reader feel that they had an inside view of a company or an area of technology.

Rest in peace Bob. One of the great early tech writers. The feeling of his writing -- the blend of fact and opinion and sense of humor, and more than anything the sense the really cared -- always felt to me like one of the seeds that developed into the blogosphere.

I all Bob would do would be writing Accidental Empires, and inspiring Simon Wardly to adapt his Commandos, Infantry and Police into Pioneers, Settlers and Town planners framework, it would still be enough to achieve immortality. Thank you, Bob!

https://blog.gardeviance.org/2015/03/on-pioneers-settlers-to...

Ah man...

Hadn't heard from him in years. Then he posted that he was going to start writing again and I was so very glad to hear it... And now...

The dude was to me what tech journalism was. Between Cringely and Dvorak leaving us, we're losing the old guard. I'm bummed.

His death was far too early. It's hard to explain how much influence Cringely had over the years, how many minds were influenced by him - and how much his humor has been assimilated into the tech industry. He will be missed.
https://www.cringely.com/bout-bob/ 
            
  On How You Can Reach Him to Tell Him He’s a Dipstick
  Robert X. Cringely
  (707) 525-9519
  (707) 525-9517 (fax)
  bob@cringely.com

  You're not supposed to die that young. That wasn't part of the deal.

Sad, and to go in a similar way to his son who he spoke about this year on his site, what are the chances.

A great a free thinker.

Sad to hear this, I watched "Triumph of the Nerds" multiple times when I was at University.

Had to login to pay my respects. His blog "this rag" as he used to call it was foundational in my professional life. And I still typed cringley.com by hand to read his posts. He had a several tragedies in his life... But now his soul can be with his children.

RIP hacker from a bygone era..

Dang - black ribbon please
De mortuis and all that, but someone has pointed out the poor track record of his later initiatives and I think the reasons for those failures are an important part of the picture. Look at his last few blog posts, outlining a radical alternative to LLMs. Read closely, and at the heart of that idea we find "assume enterprise search". But the willingness to consider radical alternatives is part of the right way to think.

I don't really understand what your comment is trying to say, but I read through the last few pages of his blog and all the posts after the first one from 2026 announcing his return seem AI generated. I think it's a shame, as I loved his writing style in "Accidental Empires" and in his earlier blog posts and columns. It's strange to me that someone who had spent most of his life writing either didn't notice or didn't care about the drop in quality from using LLMs to write.

> Look at his last few blog posts, outlining a radical alternative to LLMs. Read closely, and at the heart of that idea we find "assume enterprise search".

I found the patent for his company's technology (https://patents.google.com/patent/US20250259069A1). I always have trouble reading patents, but as far as I can tell it's basically a wrapper around commodity LLMs. The reliability improvements come from prompting the LLM to only source its data from an external database that you provide rather than from whatever it was trained on, and from prompting multiple LLMs simultaneously then doing semantic analysis on the responses to make sure they all agree. I imagine that doing this would probably reduce hallucinations, but there's no hard constraint to prevent them entirely and I'm not sure what the moat is.

The nonexistence of that external database is the crucial bit. The enterprise ontology has been the holy grail for decades. That is why I say that he was assuming the hard bit.

>But the willingness to consider radical alternatives is part of the right way to think.

That sounds liked LinkedIn speak.

While that's true, a stopped clock is right twice a day. It can simultaneously sound like LinkedIn speak and be correct.

Don't know, sounds like a total plattitude.

There's no singular "right way to think" that applies in all cases. In many cases thinking of "radical alternatives" can be a bad idea (think people falling for "alternative medicine" stuff). Or some idiot coming up with shitty "radical alternatives" because they can't accept some specific setup or status quo is better - also related to the N.I.H. mindset in software.

The rest of the right way to think is the obligation to discard radical hypotheses that don't work out. Visionaries see things that other people don't. Mostly that is because they are not there. Every so seldom, they are.

I greatly enjoyed his book Accidental Empires https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accidental_Empires

RIP Bob. Triumphs of the Nerds and Accidental Empires captured the time it was written and the future.

I remember my mother buying me "Accidental Empires" from a bargain bin at the local bookstore as a tween. I must have read it multiple times. Dot product that with "The Cuckoo's Egg" and any technical books and magazines I could get hold of, and you have the formative reading of my career.

Sad news. I’ve read his blog for forever, Bob was a total industry legend. Best wishes to his family

I had thought he had passed away earlier this year, but it was John C. Dvorak, who wrote the Infoworld industry news column before (/contemporaneously with) Mark Stephens, who adopted the name Robert X. Cringely. https://www.wired.com/1998/12/cringely/

I liked his frequently contrarian views. Pre-internet his Cringely column (which he took over from someone else) was a great source of information for those of us living far away from Silicon Valley. RIP.

This is sad news. I was born in 1989 and thus I don’t remember Cringely’s articles, but I remember watching Triumph of the Nerds in the mid-2000s. I love that documentary; it’s a nice capture of the early days of personal computing and of Silicon Valley culture of the era. I wish there were a follow-up that covered the 2000s and beyond, particularly the rise of social media, the gig economy (Uber, Lyft, AirBNB), cloud computing, big data, cryptocurrency, and generative AI.

First time i’ve heard of bob (born late 90s I guess). Had a great afternoon watching his videos. Thanks for the fun, best wishes to the family.

I’m very sorry to hear. An old copy of Accidental Empires was one of my introductions technology + capitalism

Triumph of the nerds is the reason I work in high tech. RIP to a legend.

What a great storyteller. Im surprised Triumph is mostly forgotten today. I remember being disturbed by his accounting of how Microsoft gave birth to DOS.

Damn, that’s heartbreaking. Rest in peace.

Rest in peace bob...

I read Accidental Empires when I was younger, RIP Bob.

RIP. I loved Triumph of the Nerds as a teenager.

I honestly hadn't heard of him before, and it's sad to be learning about him this way. I'll be watching Triumph of the Nerds tonight. RIP.

Dvorak, Om and Robert. Damn. Their takes on tech taught me a lot and shaped how I think about this industry. RIP.

Very sad news. My VHS box set of "Triumph of the Nerds" resides proudly on my bookshelf.

Bob was a dear friend and co-conspirator on many an adventure. He and I did everything from moonshots to nano manufacturing. I am shocked to see that he is gone. God speed Bob!

Robert X Bishop

Sad news. Reading his columns post dotcom bubble was always interesting even when I disagreed—which was often!

His takes on IBM were always interesting, especially during that turbulent time with Ginny. He is missed.

Triumph of the Nerds was my introduction to computer history as a kid. I had a dentist that learned I was into computers and he borrowed me his VHS copy. I probably would have had a very different world if I hadn't watched that, because it really turned me on to the potential. Thanks Bob (and my dentist).

I find it sad that he never got rich. Someone so energetic, articulate, and connected with the Who’s Who of Silicon Valley, getting the inside track on everything (especially in his early years), didn’t become fabulously wealthy. There may have been opportunities for him to be an early investor in a meteoric startup, or becoming a co-founder or adviser or board member. But didn’t happen.

Is getting rich important?

That's a bit sad to read, to me he seemed to have been living a very rich life, albeit filled with lots of unfair and sad things happening to him. But seems he got to do what he loved doing, with people he loved, and that's pretty much as rich as you can get in life. Not every one has "make bank account have lots of money" as a priority in life, and if you're aiming for actual happiness, that's probably the way to go, as Cringely has demonstrated to us.

Oh man this is really sad to me. End of an Era. His documentaries fueled me so much in the 90s and 2000s. I loved his stuff and his blogs.

Did an amazing job documenting the computer revolution and the internet revolution.

RIP.

May his memory be a blessing

I immigrated to the US to work in Silicon Valley directly because of Triumph of the Nerds that I watched in PBS. I have a life that I could never have achieved in my home country and I am grateful to Bob Cringely for this. May he rest in peace.

I loved "I, Cringely"

I remember in the very early days of ZeroTier him stopping by our tiny coworking office in SoCal (we weren't scattered all over yet). He said it piqued his interest because it was "something that should have been built 10 or 15 years ago." (I'm paraphrasing. This was around 2015.)

He belongs to the old Silicon Valley. I wasn't there in those days and have never lived there, but I miss it.

It was back when SV was genuinely creative and largely positive in its attitude toward people and the future. It emerged from the ethos of places like SRI's "augmented human intelligence" lab and things like the Whole Earth Catalog and the Homebrew Computer Club.

Of course I'm well aware of the other origin story, the one that goes back to WWII and the defense industry. They're both true in different ways, but I think the ideas I mentioned above were the ones that came to dominate for a while.

articles.title: Run Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (125B) on consumer hardware (RTX 4090) at 100T/s
articles.full_content:
English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · Deutsch · Français · Español · Português

Run a 125-billion-parameter AI model on your own gaming PC
NVIDIA or AMD graphics card (12 GB or more) · Windows or Linux · free and open source


A voxel pagoda garden, 1 shot prompt running on an RTX 5070 with Strata (IQ3_S, 128K context) · full video (49 s)

Strata runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a normal PC. This is a large, smart AI model that usually needs a server. It chats, writes code, reads pictures and works with your apps and coding agents. Nothing leaves your PC.

We measured it on two ordinary gaming PCs. A token is about ¾ of a word.

  • Writes answers: how fast the reply appears in a short chat. 60 tokens per second is faster than you can read.
  • Reads your prompt: how fast it takes in what you send (here a 32K-token document, code or chat history).
NVIDIA: RTX 5070 (12 GB), Ryzen 5 7600, 64 GB RAM AMD: RX 9070 XT (16 GB), Ryzen 9 3900X, 47 GB RAM
Size Writes answers Reads your prompt
Q2_0 94 tokens/s2,650 tokens/s
IQ2_XS 79 tokens/s2,090 tokens/s
IQ3_XXS 62 tokens/s1,750 tokens/s
IQ3_S 53 tokens/s1,620 tokens/s
Coder 55 tokens/s2,180 tokens/s
Size Writes answers Reads your prompt
Q2_0 60 tokens/s1,160 tokens/s
IQ2_XS 52 tokens/s1,110 tokens/s
Coder 44 tokens/s1,420 tokens/s

NVIDIA: Q2_0 with engine 0.1.36, the other rows with 0.1.26 (4K answers, 32K prompts). The full tables are in DETAILS.md. A card with more VRAM is faster: an RTX 3090 (24 GB) should write about 100-140 tokens per second. Long chats and other cards: speed of each model, community results.


Strata is free. If it runs well on your PC, a coffee keeps the work on it going.

Graphics card NVIDIA GeForce RTX 20, 30, 40 or 50 series, or AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT / XTX, RX 7800 XT / 7700 XT, RX 9060 XT, RX 9070 / 9070 XT, Radeon AI PRO R9700 or RX 6800 / 6900 series. It needs 12 GB of VRAM or more.
RAM 32 GB or more. Your RAM decides which model fits. 64 GB runs every size.
Disk About 80 GB free. Use an SSD if you can: the first start is much faster.
System Windows 10 / 11 or Linux, and a current graphics driver from NVIDIA or AMD.

The installer sets up everything else. Two or three cards can share the model (multi-GPU).

Experimental, written and tested by community members on their own machines:

  • Older graphics cards (Tesla P40 / V100, GTX 10, Radeon VII / MI50, RX 6700 XT, RX 5500 XT): Older GPUs.
  • Intel Arc, built from source on Linux: Intel Arc.
  • Older processors without AVX2: they work, but slowly. Older CPUs.

The full list: docs/INSTALL.md.

Do you use an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, ...)? Paste this into it:

      
Set up Strata on this PC for me: https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata - follow docs/AI_SETUP.md in that repository.

It checks your graphics card, RAM and disk and picks the model that fits. Then it installs and starts it and tells you how to connect your apps. AI tools can also install, start and stop Strata through its MCP server.

Download Strata and unzip it (or 

git clone
it). Windows: double-click 
START-HERE.bat
. Linux: run 
./setup.sh
 in the Strata folder.

The steps are the same for NVIDIA and AMD. The installer finds your card and sets up the right engine for it. It asks you a few questions:

  • which model and which size,
  • how much context (how much text the model keeps in mind),
  • whether it should read pictures.

Press Enter each time for the recommended answer. Then it downloads the model (about 70 GB) and starts it. If the download stops, run it again: it continues where it left off. Your browser opens the Strata app at 

http://127.0.0.1:8080
.

While the model starts, your PC can be slow or stop responding for 1-3 minutes (longest the first time). Strata loads 35-55 GB into your RAM and locks part of it for the graphics card. This is normal. Wait, and don't close the window. The window shows what Strata is doing.

Next time, run 

START-HERE.bat
(or 
./setup.sh
) again. It starts right away and downloads nothing twice. Close its window to stop the model. 
UPDATE.bat
(
./update.sh
) updates Strata without starting it. Updating, Docker, several cards, where the files go and every option: docs/INSTALL.md.

The installer recommends one for your RAM. The same model comes in several sizes, compressed more or less. Smaller sizes are faster. Larger sizes are a bit smarter.

Your RAM Take Why
32 GB Coder it fits 32 GB, and it is made for code (with a 24 GB card, Q2_0 and IQ2_XS run too)
48 GB IQ2_XS (or Q2_0, the fastest) the larger sizes do not fit
64 GB IQ2_XS (recommended), or IQ3_XXS / IQ3_S every size fits; IQ3_S is the best and the slowest
96 GB or more IQ3_S, or Unsloth's UD-IQ4_XS (~4-bit) room for the largest sizes with everything else open
  • Coder: a coding version with half of the experts removed. It reaches 91% of the full model's SWE-bench Verified score (measured by its authors) and fits 32 GB of RAM. It is weaker outside code, including Chinese and other CJK text (#438). For those, take Q2_0, IQ2_XS or IQ3_S, which keep every expert.
  • Swift 1.5: a fine-tune that thinks for a much shorter time before it answers. You get the answer sooner, at about the same quality.
  • Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS: Unsloth's ~4-bit version, between IQ3_S and UD-Q4_K_XL in quality. A 94 GB download. With less than ~80 GB of RAM, Strata reads part of it from the SSD while it answers, so it is slower there (an NVMe SSD helps).
  • Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL (experimental): the closest to the full model. But Strata reads most of it from the SSD while it answers, so it writes only 7-8.5 tokens/s on a 64 GB PC.
  • OrcaRouter's Uncensored IQ3_XXS: you set it up by hand. It is not in the installer's menu.

Sizes, downloads and what fits where: docs/MODELS.md. To add another model later, run 

SETUP.bat
(Linux: 
./setup.sh --setup
).


The Strata app's Monitor (left) while a coding agent writes the pagoda garden from the video (right)

  • In the browser: open 
    http://127.0.0.1:8080
    . It has Chat, a live Monitor of the model and your GPU/CPU/RAM, and About with the settings and addresses.
  • Your apps and coding agents: add an "OpenAI-compatible" provider with the base URL 
    http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
    . Any API key and any model name work.
    • Apps that use Anthropic's API: 
      http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/messages
      (Claude Code: 
      ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080
      ).
    • Codex CLI and other apps that use the OpenAI Responses API: 
      /v1/responses
      (setup).
  • Thinking: choose off, low, medium or high in the chat menu or in your app's "reasoning effort". Off is the fastest. High is best for hard questions.
  • Pictures: say yes to "Images?" in setup. Then click Picture in the chat, or attach pictures in your app. AMD cards read pictures on Linux through the processor; on Windows they can't yet.
  • From your phone or another PC: 
    START-HERE.bat --setup --host 0.0.0.0 --api-key <secret>
    . Always set a key.
  • One request at a time: by default Strata answers one request, and the others wait. To answer several at once, set 
    "parallel": 2
    (BATCHING.md). On a 12 GB card this makes each answer slower.
  • Long prompts: Strata reads the first message of a chat in full, about 1 minute per 30,000 tokens. Follow-up messages start in seconds.

More: where your chats are stored, the API.

  • My PC froze the first time Strata started. This is normal while it loads the model. Wait, and don't close the window. Still frozen after 10 minutes? Restart the PC, close other programs and try again, or pick a smaller size.
  • It stopped while downloading or installing. Run 
    START-HERE.bat
    (or 
    ./setup.sh
    ) again. It continues where it stopped.
  • It's very slow and the disk light keeps blinking, or it says "the engine stopped unexpectedly". Your PC does not have enough free RAM. Close other programs (browsers use a lot), or pick a smaller size (Q2_0 or IQ2_XS).
  • It says port 8080 is already in use. Strata is already running. Look for its window.

More problems and their fixes: docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md. Still stuck? Open an issue and attach 

strata-<model>.log
from the Strata folder. Found a security problem? Report it privately: SECURITY.md.

Models like this one usually run on servers with hundreds of gigabytes of graphics memory. Your graphics card has 12-24 GB. Strata makes the model fit by sharing the work across your whole PC. Think of a kitchen: the things you use all the time stay on the counter, and the rest waits in the pantry.

  • The model is a team of 24,576 small specialists ("experts"). Each word needs only 10 of them.
  • Your graphics card keeps the few thousand experts that are used most often. Your RAM holds all of them, and your processor works on the rest at the same time. Your SSD holds a big lookup table.
  • Guess, then check: a small helper guesses the next few words. The big model checks them all at once. You get the same answer, 1.6-1.8x sooner.
  • Long texts are read in big pieces (up to 8,192 tokens at a time), at over 1,000 tokens per second.

The longer explanation: docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md. Every part and its numbers: the details and the paper.

The model is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by the Qwen team. It was compressed by ISTA-DASLab, UkisAI (Swift 1.5) and Unsloth. Strata uses parts of llama.cpp / ggml. All credits: docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md. Strata is open source under the MIT License. A few parts and every model have their own licenses (which ones).

Strata is free and open source. If it is useful to you, you can support its development:

articles.title: Turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and get its disk space back
articles.full_content:
Turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 and remove its downloaded models.

macOS 27 no longer has a single switch for Apple Intelligence, and its models stay on disk after the features are turned off. RemoveMacAI turns the features off, removes the models and prevents macOS from downloading them again. All changes can be reverted.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash

The script downloads the latest release, verifies its SHA-256 checksum and runs it from a temporary directory. Nothing is installed.

Every release is built from its tag by GitHub Actions and carries a build provenance attestation. To check that a download came from this repository's source:

gh attestation verify removemacai-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -R omlahore/RemoveMacAI

With Homebrew:

brew install omlahore/tap/removemacai
removemacai

RemoveMacAI shows the current state and asks for confirmation. It then opens System Settings to install its configuration profile, which macOS requires the user to approve, and removes the models.

Command Description 
removemacai
 Show the current state, then turn Apple Intelligence off
removemacai status
 Show each feature and the size of the models on disk
removemacai off --keep <features>
 Leave the listed features on
removemacai off --dry-run
 Show the changes without applying them
removemacai revert
 Undo all changes
removemacai features
 List the feature names accepted by 
--keep

To revert with the one-line installer:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash -s revert

Features turned off: Siri (including "Hey Siri" and the menu bar icon), Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, summaries in Mail, Messages, Safari, Notes and notifications, Mail smart replies, inline text predictions, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up and Xcode predictive code completion.

Models removed: the Apple Intelligence foundation models and the models for image generation and Genmoji, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up and Xcode code completion.

  • A configuration profile applies Apple's restriction keys for Apple Intelligence and forces the settings that have no restriction key.
  • Models are removed through Apple's asset service. System Integrity Protection stays enabled and no files under 
    /System
    are modified directly.
  • The profile redirects the download of each removed model to a closed local port, so macOS does not download it again.
  • Removing the profile restores the previous settings. macOS downloads the models again when a feature needs them.

RemoveMacAI makes no network requests and collects no data.

Does dictation still work? Yes. Dictation is a separate setting, and its speech models are not removed.

Do macOS updates undo the changes? No. The profile, including the download block, persists across updates.

Storage settings still lists Apple Intelligence after the models were deleted. Apple's asset service releases the models right away, but macOS deletes the files on its own schedule. Until then, System Settings > General > Storage keeps counting them under Apple Intelligence.

Why is a process named Siri still running? In macOS 27 the Spotlight window runs as a process named Siri. Some system services also stay loaded; they are protected by System Integrity Protection.

What stops working? The features listed above, apps that use Apple's on-device models (the Foundation Models framework and the Use Model action in Shortcuts), Visual Intelligence and natural-language editing in Calendar.

Apple silicon.

macOS Status
27 Supported, tested on 27.0. On 27.0.1, use 0.2.3 or later.
26 and earlier Not supported

Run 

removemacai revert
, then 
brew uninstall removemacai
if it was installed with Homebrew.

RemoveMacAI is built on pared, a complete working tool by 4evy that first mapped the asset service, the model sets and several of the settings keys. Its license is in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.

articles.title: Improper redaction reveals Google Data Center water and electricity usage
articles.full_content:
UPDATE: Improper redaction reveals Lincoln’s Google Data Center water and electricity usage

Nebraska data centers submit 2026 annual report

LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN) - Nebraska data centers are required to turn in an annual report to Nebraska’s Department of Water, Energy, and Environment, but some state statutes are preventing the public from seeing just how much electricity and water data centers are using.

The Google Data Center in Lincoln, named Agate LLC, claimed their electricity usage and water usage were trade secret information, citing Neb. Rev. State §§ 81-1527; 84-712.05 and NAC TITLE 115, CH. 2. In fact, Google did this for all three data centers, including their sites in Omaha and Papillion.

However, using a computer cursor to highlight the redacted text box in the report to DWEE, then copying and pasting it into a separate document reveals that Agate LLC is reporting 52.65 megawatts of electricity during peak electrical demand and 13.299 megagallons of water between cooling towers, evaporative systems and site operations in the last year. That totals out to 13 million gallons of water.

For context, 13 million gallons is enough to fill around 20 Olympic-size swimming pools, and is less than half of what the City of Lincoln reports using on Sept. 29.

The six data centers reporting as of Sept. 30 show a total use of 765 million gallons of water last year, enough water to fill 1,159.93 Olympic-size swimming pools.

More improper redaction shows that the data center using the most water annually is Fireball Group LLC, the Google Data Center in Papillion. Fireball LLC reports 547.88 megagallons for their 2025 Annual Water Consumption.

10/11 filed a public record request Sept. 30 to see redacted information from Agate LLC’s report.

Further improper redaction reveals exactly how much of a 2025 tax refund Google data centers expect.

Google’s reports state that data centers only “utilize or expect to utilize” sales and use tax exemptions under the Nebraska Advantage Act. Reports state no rebates have been received for that program to date, nor have any incentive payments been received, or are expected to be received under the ImagiNE Nebraska Act.

Agate LLC reports expecting a refund of $55,822,472 from 2025 taxes. Fireball LLC is expecting a refund of $39,171,573.39 from 2025 taxes. Westwood Solutions LLC, the Google-owned data center in Omaha, is expecting a refund of $22,558,881 from 2025 taxes.

Documents submitted by Agate LLC show that the gross floor area is 288,530 square feet - about five football fields.

The Department of Water, Energy, and Environment Data Center Task Force is overseeing the execution of Governor Jim Pillen’s July 20th Executive Order requiring data centers in the state to self-report their impact on Nebraska’s resources; primarily water, power grids and local infrastructure.

Usage reports are due by Sept. 30. Submitted reports can be read here, simply enter “DCR” into the “DEQ Program” field.
